name: Communitarian Governance Systems
region: Global (Sub-Saharan Africa, Southeast Asia, Polynesia, Indigenous Americas)
summary: Governance frameworks grounded in collective welfare and relational personhood, where authority derives from community consensus and leaders serve as stewards rather than rulers.

claims.statement: Ubuntu-based governance in southern Africa, gotong royong in Indonesia, and village council systems across Polynesia represent independent convergent evolution toward communitarian models
Communitarian governance systems show greater resilience to external shocks than centralised hierarchies, maintaining social cohesion through colonial and post-colonial disruption
Modern communitarian political theory draws directly on these Indigenous precedents, not solely on Western philosophical traditions

evidence.source: Gyekye (1997) Tradition and Modernity: Philosophical Reflections on the African Experience, Oxford UP
Bowen (1986) On the Political Construction of Tradition: Gotong Royong in Indonesia, Journal of Asian Studies 45(3)
Mamdani (1996) Citizen and Subject: Contemporary Africa and the Legacy of Late Colonialism, Princeton UP
Samoan matai (chief) system oral governance traditions documented by Mead (1928, 1969)
Bell (2016) Communitarianism, in Zalta (ed.) Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
